meta.title: The Kids Who Hacked the World, Part 4: Kevin Mitnick, America's Most Wanted Hacker
meta.working_title: The Boy Who Hacked People, Not Computers (The Kids Who Hacked the World, Part 4)
meta.device: A magician's stage: every con opens with a curtain and a playing card that flips to reveal the trick ('the bus ticket', 'the phone call', 'the guard'), and a WANTED poster that gets bigger every act.
meta.style: Retro crime caper in the house 2D style, Gumball/t-shirt character style (same as Parts 1-3). Painted plates: 1970s Los Angeles bus depot, payphones, a phone-company building at night, a 1980s computer room with tape drives, a burger joint, a San Diego supercomputer lab, a Raleigh apartment, a courtroom packed with press. Warm 70s browns and 80s neon green screens. Real people stylised with no likeness. Social engineering described only as 'pretending to be staff' and 'asking nicely'; no technical how-to. SFX under the VO (payphone coins, dial tones, modem screech, tape reels, gavel), music at combine.
meta.source: English compilation transcript 'The Kids Who Hacked the World', segment 5 (~5,600 words), largely from Mitnick's memoir Ghost in the Wires (his own account, flagged) plus press coverage. Sponsor reads cut; technical steps removed. Fully rewritten.

shots.vo: February 1995, Raleigh, North Carolina. FBI agents knock on an apartment door. Is he Kevin Mitnick? He says no.
shots.visual: An apartment door; agents in windbreakers; a man in the doorway shaking his head.

shots.vo: In the pocket of an old ski jacket, they find a pay stub with his real name on it. After more than two years on the run, America's most wanted hacker is caught.
shots.visual: A crumpled pay stub pulled from a jacket; the name circled.

shots.vo: His secret weapon was rarely code. It was people. A friendly voice, a confident story, and staff who wanted to help.
shots.visual: A magician's stage; a curtain pulls back to reveal a telephone.
Title over the stage.
shots.onscreen: THE KIDS WHO HACKED THE WORLD · PART 4

shots.vo: Los Angeles, 1975. Kevin is 12 and loves magic tricks. What fascinates him most is how easily people believe what they're shown.
shots.visual: A boy at a magic show, watching the audience instead of the magician.

shots.vo: He rides buses all summer. By his own account, he chats up a driver about a 'school project' and learns where the ticket punch is sold.
shots.visual: A bus; the boy chatting to a smiling driver.

shots.vo: Unused transfer tickets get thrown away at the depot. With a punch and the spares, he rides for free all summer.
shots.visual: A bin full of ticket booklets; a boy punching a ticket, grinning.

shots.vo: In high school a friend shows him how one phone call to the phone company can get an unlisted number. Kevin is hooked.
shots.visual: Two teens at a payphone; a phone book with a blank line filling in.

shots.vo: He joins the 'phone phreaks', teens who explore the phone network. He calls phone-company offices pretending to be an employee, and learns how everything works.
shots.visual: A teen with a phone in each hand; org-chart cards filling in on the wall.
shots.anim: Org chart builds card by card.

shots.vo: Soon he can get almost any unlisted number. In his memoir he says he got Bruce Springsteen's, just for fun.
shots.visual: A star-shaped card with a phone number blurred.

shots.vo: At 17 he and two friends talk their way past a guard into a phone-company building, and walk out with operating manuals.
shots.visual: A night-time office building; three teens strolling past a guard who waves them in.

shots.vo: A friend brags about it. Kevin is arrested and tried as a juvenile: a psychological evaluation and a year of probation.
shots.visual: Handcuffs; a juvenile court; a PROBATION stamp.

shots.vo: In the mid-1980s he tries to go straight, and gets a programming job at a phone company. After nine days, a background check gets him fired.
shots.visual: An office desk being packed into a box; a FIRED note.

shots.vo: This is the era of the movie WarGames, about a teen who nearly starts a nuclear war with a computer. Hackers become a national fear.
shots.visual: A cinema marquee; newspaper headlines about hacker panic.

shots.vo: By night Kevin and his friend Lenny go after DEC, then the second biggest computer maker in the world. Their goal: the secret source code of its operating system.
shots.visual: A 1980s computer room with big cabinets and tape reels.

shots.vo: Once again, a phone call does most of the work: Kevin poses as a DEC employee and talks a staff member into letting them in.
shots.visual: Kevin at two payphones at once; a curtain flips to show 'THE PHONE CALL'.

shots.vo: They copy the code bit by bit and end up with around 30 tapes of it. Not to sell it. Just to have it.
shots.visual: A stack of old magnetic tapes growing to the ceiling.

shots.vo: Kevin and Lenny turn it into a game: who can break into the other's workplace first. The prize: a fancy dinner. Kevin keeps winning. Lenny stops paying.
shots.visual: A scoreboard: KEVIN 5, LENNY 1; a restaurant bill.

shots.vo: Kevin plays a prank on Lenny's employer. Lenny is furious, confesses to his boss, and goes to the FBI.
shots.visual: Lenny at his boss's desk, pointing; an FBI badge slides in.

shots.vo: 1988. Lenny meets Kevin in a car park, and agents are waiting. 'Why did you do this to me?' Kevin asks. 'Because you're a menace to society.'
shots.visual: A dark parking garage; agents emerging; a quote card.

shots.vo: Prosecutors tell a judge he could start a nuclear war by whistling into a phone. Kevin says he laughed. He's held in solitary confinement before trial, and gets a year in prison.
shots.visual: A courtroom; a dramatic missile cartoon over a phone; a solitary cell.
shots.anim: Missile doodle pops; cell door clangs.

shots.vo: Out of prison, he can't find work, and gets bored. Then a hacker calling himself Eric Heinz gets in touch, bragging about secret phone-company systems.
shots.visual: Kevin at a kitchen table; a phone ringing with a mysterious caller ID.

shots.vo: Kevin gets into a phone-company testing system that can listen in on calls. But something about Heinz feels wrong.
shots.visual: Headphones beside a glowing screen; a question mark over a business card.

shots.vo: Digging into his phone records, Kevin finds Heinz has been calling the FBI. He's an informant.
shots.visual: A phone bill with 'FBI' highlighted.

shots.vo: In 1992, with a new arrest warrant out, Kevin vanishes. He lives under false names in different cities for more than two years.
shots.visual: A map of the US with a dotted line hopping between cities; the WANTED poster grows.
shots.anim: Dotted line hops city to city.

shots.vo: Christmas 1994. Someone breaks into the computers of Tsutomu Shimomura, a top security researcher in San Diego, and steals his files.
shots.visual: A long-haired researcher in shorts at a supercomputer lab, staring at an alert.

shots.vo: Then come mocking voicemails in a fake kung-fu-movie voice. Shimomura takes it personally, and teams up with the FBI.
shots.visual: An answering machine blinking; a cartoon karate pose on a speech bubble.

shots.vo: With help from an internet provider, they trace the intruder's connections to Raleigh, North Carolina, and watch him online in real time.
shots.visual: A US map with a line zooming to Raleigh; a screen showing typed text appearing live.

shots.vo: That brings agents to the apartment door, and the pay stub in the ski jacket. In court, Kevin passes Shimomura and says, 'I respect your skills.'
shots.visual: A packed courtroom; two figures nodding at each other.

shots.vo: Supporters rally with 'Free Kevin' campaigns. Claims of nearly 300 million dollars in damage shrink to 4,125 dollars in restitution.
shots.visual: A 'FREE KEVIN' bumper sticker; a number shrinking from $300M to $4,125.

shots.vo: In 1999 he pleads guilty to some charges. With time already served, he spends about five years behind bars, and walks out in January 2000, banned from computers for three years.
shots.visual: A prison gate opening; a 'NO COMPUTERS' card.

shots.vo: He reinvents himself as a security consultant. Companies pay him to break in. One word made the difference, he wrote: authorisation.
shots.visual: Kevin on a conference stage; a big word 'AUTHORISATION'.

shots.vo: Kevin Mitnick died in July 2023, aged 59. Next: a 15-year-old in Miami who broke into NASA and the Pentagon.
shots.visual: A single spotlight on an empty stage; then a NEXT card with a rocket.
End card.
shots.onscreen: THE KIDS WHO HACKED THE WORLD · PART 5 NEXT

hooks: America's most wanted hacker was caught because of a pay stub in a ski jacket.
Kevin Mitnick rarely needed code. He just picked up the phone and pretended to be staff.

fixes: Personal anecdotes (bus tickets, Springsteen number, DEC game) are from Mitnick's memoir Ghost in the Wires and flagged as his account.
DEC arrest December 1988; sentenced 1989 to 1 year (plus halfway house).
Fugitive from late 1992; arrested Raleigh 15 Feb 1995.
1999 plea; total ~5 years in custody including pre-trial; restitution $4,125; released 21 Jan 2000.
'Whistle into a phone and launch nukes' claim is Mitnick's account of prosecutors' arguments; worded as such.
Shimomura voicemails' authorship disputed (Littman); not stated as Mitnick's.
All technical steps (spawn commands, IP spoofing, backdoors) removed; methods described as phone pretexting only.
